clue.text: Warmer on entering flat in south- central England?

parts.note: Beds is the short form of Bedfordshire, a county north of London

indicators.note: the word for 'on' goes into the word for flat

parts.note: a pad is slang for a flat or home
re means on or concerning, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: A puzzled query about whether someone warmer is settling into an apartment somewhere in the English home counties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warmer' looks like a comparative adjective but is a noun, a bed covering; 'in' is only a link word. Bedfordshire is a county just north of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A cover laid over a bed keeps the sleeper warm, so the quilt is a warmer by description.

clue.text: So-called rubbish artist

indicators.note: so-called signals a word as it is called out, by its sound

parts.note: bosh is a dated word for nonsense or rubbish

explanation.surface: A critic sneers at a painter whose work is supposedly rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Hieronymus of that surname was the Dutch painter of The Garden of Earthly Delights.

clue.text: Barking, mog admits arrogance

indicators.note: barking means mad, so the letters go crazy and are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cat is accused of being haughty, and the barking dog makes it confess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' looks like a dog's noise or the London district, but it means mad and signals the anagram of MOG ADMITS.
explanation.definitionFit: Insisting one's own opinions are beyond question is a form of overbearing arrogance.

clue.text: Where American car may be a great deal below average, man!

indicators.note: in a down clue the word for a great deal sits below the other pieces

parts.note: par is the standard or average level
a king is a man, a piece in chess
a lot is a great deal

explanation.surface: An exclamation that a US car can be bought at a bargain, well below the usual price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a great deal below average' reads as a price, but 'deal' is part of LOT and 'below' just places it under PAR and KING.
explanation.definitionFit: In American English an open space set aside for leaving vehicles is called by this name.

clue.text: In the end, provocative footwear used, oddly, for pastoral work

indicators.note: in the end picks only the final letter of provocative

parts.note: a clog is a wooden shoe

indicators.note: oddly takes the odd-numbered letters of used, the first and third

explanation.surface: Provocative footwear ends up being used for some rustic farm labour.
explanation.definitionFit: A short poem set among shepherds, like Virgil's, is a classic piece of pastoral writing.

clue.text: Is card between pair of diamonds swell?

indicators.note: between places the other pieces inside the two diamond letters

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for diamonds in card games, so a pair gives two
a ten is a playing card

explanation.surface: A card player asks whether a card sitting between two diamonds makes a great hand.
explanation.definitionFit: To swell is to bloat or expand outwards, as a stomach does.

clue.text: Old Czech dissident, keep left

parts.note: to have is to keep or hold

explanation.surface: An instruction to stay on the left, attached to a figure from Czech history.
explanation.definitionFit: Vaclav, the playwright jailed under communism, later became president of Czechoslovakia.

clue.text: Politician dismissing case of rabble

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outer letters, which are sent away

parts.note: a shower is British slang for a useless bunch, a rabble

explanation.surface: A politician waves aside a legal action brought by the mob.
explanation.walkthrough: SHOWER is British slang for a hopeless crowd; losing its outer letters leaves the surname of Geoffrey, Thatcher's chancellor and foreign secretary.
explanation.definitionFit: Geoffrey, whose resignation speech helped topple Margaret Thatcher, was a senior Conservative minister.

clue.text: See 24
Point penned by editor in politician's comic

indicators.note: in places the letters for an edited point inside the chancellor's name

parts.note: Nigel Lawson was Thatcher's Chancellor of the Exchequer; the 's links him to the comic

indicators.note: penned by means held inside, as in a pen

parts.note: S, south, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: An editor makes a point about a politician's joke.
explanation.walkthrough: Nigel Lawson was a Conservative chancellor; Les Dawson was a deadpan British TV comedian famous for mother-in-law jokes and bad piano playing.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lancashire funny man was a well-known stand-up comedian of 1970s and 80s British television.

clue.text: See 26
When twin has dropped in, visiting house, passing comment

indicators.note: visiting puts the inner pieces into the house, as guests go into it

parts.note: the Lords is the upper House of Parliament
as can mean when, as in 'as he left'

indicators.note: has dropped means the letters of the word in fall out of twin

parts.note: taken as written before the deletion

explanation.surface: A remark made as a twin pops in to someone's home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has dropped in' looks like a visit, but 'in' is the letters removed from TWIN; 'passing' is about dying, not walking by.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's final utterance before death is a comment made at their passing.

clue.text: Where test may be good after racket covered up by politician

indicators.note: covered up by puts the noise and the good inside the politician's name

parts.note: Denis Healey was a Labour Chancellor of the Exchequer

indicators.note: after places G behind DIN

parts.note: a din is a loud noise, a racket

explanation.surface: A politician hushes up a scandal where a good test of character might happen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'racket' and 'test' suggest tennis or exams; the test is a cricket Test match, played at this ground in Leeds.
explanation.definitionFit: The Leeds cricket ground regularly hosts England's Test matches against touring sides.

clue.text: Star reversing in luggage van

indicators.note: reversing says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A celebrity backs into a train's baggage carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the brightest points of light in the night sky, in the constellation Lyra.

clue.text: A blunder with fee almost embarrassed — to be paid back

indicators.note: embarrassed means thrown into confusion, so the letters are mixed up
almost means the word fee loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Charging a fee in error is embarrassing, so the money has to be returned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts FEE to FE; 'embarrassed' then rearranges A BLUNDER with FE.
explanation.definitionFit: Money that can be returned to the payer is owed back, as with a deposit.

clue.text: Beside fire, quivering with anticipation

parts.note: at can mean beside, as in 'at the door'
an ingle is a fireplace or hearth fire

explanation.surface: Someone sitting by the fireside, trembling with excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: INGLE, as in inglenook, is an old word for a hearth fire.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling a thrill of eager excitement all over is to be in a nervous excited state.

clue.text: Not believing when a jerk admits crime

indicators.note: admits means lets in, so the crime goes inside the jerk

parts.note: a tic is an involuntary twitch or jerk
a heist is a robbery

explanation.surface: A sceptic is unconvinced when some idiot confesses to an offence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jerk' reads as an insult for a person, but it is a twitch, TIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Rejecting the existence of any god is the stance of one without religious faith.

clue.text: Sprinkles powder on tidied hair, both at the back and fringes

indicators.note: both at the back takes the last letter of each of the two words

parts.note: edges are fringes or borders

explanation.surface: Someone dusts powder over freshly combed hair, back and fringe alike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fringes' poses as part of a hairstyle but means EDGES.
explanation.definitionFit: A cook coats food with a dusting of flour or sugar by shaking it over the top.

clue.text: Sweet thing, a Scot unfortunately beset by wind

indicators.note: beset by means surrounded, so the jumbled letters sit within the wind

parts.note: a gale is a strong wind

indicators.note: unfortunately signals a word that has come to grief, rearranged

explanation.surface: A sweet-natured Scot battered by a storm, poor soul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' poses as a description of the Scot, but 'Sweet thing' is the definition: a sugar.
explanation.definitionFit: This simple sugar, found in milk, is a kind of sweet compound.

clue.text: Politician serving suggestion with eggs, reportedly?

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard, so the words are spoken out

parts.note: a breakfast with eggs might be offered as 'ham and' eggs

explanation.surface: A politician is said to have recommended a dish with eggs.
explanation.walkthrough: Philip of that surname was a recent Conservative chancellor; 'ham and' eggs, said quickly, gives his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip, Chancellor of the Exchequer under Theresa May, is a British Conservative politician.

clue.text: Politician's baby

definitions.meaning: Alistair, Labour Chancellor of the Exchequer under Gordon Brown
baby is an endearment for a loved one, like sweetheart

explanation.definitionFit: Alistair is a Labour former chancellor, and the word is also a pet name like sweetheart.

clue.text: Self-pitying politician, finally removed

indicators.note: finally removed means the last letter is taken away

parts.note: Reginald Maudling was a Conservative Chancellor and Home Secretary

explanation.surface: A politician feeling sorry for himself after at last being sacked.
explanation.definitionFit: Being tearfully sentimental and sorry for oneself, often when drunk, is this mood.

clue.text: Island where politician arrived without me

parts.note: John Major was the Conservative prime minister after Thatcher

indicators.note: without means the word me is taken out

parts.note: came means arrived

explanation.surface: A traveller names the island a politician reached without them.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest of Spain's Balearic Islands, a popular Mediterranean holiday destination.

clue.text: Sinister character I back

parts.note: ago means back in time, as in 'years back'

explanation.surface: Someone admits to supporting a villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' looks like a verb, to support, but means AGO.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello's scheming ensign in Shakespeare is a classic villain of the stage.

clue.text: A pain going uphill, plod

indicators.note: in a down clue going uphill means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: a drag is a bore or pain

explanation.surface: A trudge up a hill is painful work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plod' looks like a verb but is British slang for a police officer; the answer is an Irish police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Plod is British slang for the police, and this is a member of Ireland's police force.

clue.text: Before getting squeezed round back of cupboard, leaning to one side

parts.note: pre is the prefix meaning before

indicators.note: round means the squeezed word goes around the letter

parts.note: juiced means squeezed, as with an orange

indicators.note: back of takes the final letter of cupboard

explanation.surface: Something gets crammed into a cupboard and ends up tilting over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaning to one side' sounds physical, but it means biased.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaning towards one side of an argument is being biased, holding a preconceived view.

clue.text: Europeans dressed up in lederhosen, a disaster

indicators.note: in a down clue up says the hidden letters read from bottom to top
in says the letters are found inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Some Europeans in leather shorts look a fashion catastrophe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dressed up in lederhosen' paints a costume, but 'up' reverses SENAD hidden across LEDERHOSEN, A DISASTER.
explanation.definitionFit: People from Denmark are Scandinavian Europeans.

clue.text: Top always top in dominant European country

parts.note: a cap is a top, as on a bottle
ever means always

indicators.note: top in picks the first letter of the word dominant

explanation.surface: A European nation that always comes out on top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' does two jobs in two places: first as CAP, then as 'top in', the first letter of 'dominant'.
explanation.definitionFit: The island nation off West Africa is an independent sovereign state.

clue.text: Other art, I suspect, is rougher

indicators.note: suspect as an adjective means dodgy, so the letters are unsound and rearranged

explanation.surface: A critic suspects that some other artwork is cruder.
explanation.definitionFit: A voice that is hoarser or more gravelly sounds harsher, from the throat.

clue.text: Politician 18 hit once

parts.note: Gordon, Labour prime minister from 2007 to 2010
18 stands for the answer at 18 down, a pet name, here swapped for another endearment like honey

explanation.surface: A politician, his name linked to 18, struck in the past.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a 1971 Rolling Stones single; 'hit' looks like a verb but means a chart success.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rolling Stones' 1971 single reached the top of the charts, making it a hit in its day.

clue.text: County politician ousts king

indicators.note: ousts means the king is thrown out of the politician's name

parts.note: Ken Clarke was a long-serving Conservative chancellor
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A local politician overthrows the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a county on the west coast of Ireland, home of the Cliffs of Moher.

clue.text: Awkward without 18?

parts.note: the answer at 18 down is the surname of the Victorian lighthouse heroine who rowed to a wreck in 1838; her first name is used
less means without, as in 'a year less a day'

explanation.surface: A clumsy question: is this what you are without 18?
explanation.walkthrough: The 1838 Northumberland lighthouse heroine shares her surname with 18 down; her first name plus LESS gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking elegance or poise of movement is being clumsy and ungainly.
